units.text: INT. HUSBAND - CONTINUOUS

How absurdly English you are! The English think that a cheque-book can solve every problem in life. Why, my dear Arthur, I have very much more money than you have, and quite as much as Robert Chiltern has got hold of. Money is not what I want.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: What do you want then, Mrs. Cheveley?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Why don’t you call me Laura?
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: I don’t like the name.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: You used to adore it.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Yes: that’s why.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: MRS. CHEVELEY motions to him to sit down beside her .
He smiles , and does so .
Arthur, you loved me once.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Yes.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: And you asked me to be your wife.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: That was the natural result of my loving you.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: And you threw me over because you saw, or said you saw, poor old Lord Mortlake trying to have a violent flirtation with me in the conservatory at Tenby.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: I am under the impression that my lawyer settled that matter with you on certain terms . . . dictated by yourself.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: At that time I was poor; you were rich.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Quite so. That is why you pretended to love me.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Shrugging her shoulders .

Poor old Lord Mortlake, who had only two topics of conversation, his gout and his wife! I never could quite make out which of the two he was talking about. He used the most horrible language about them both. Well, you were silly, Arthur. Why, Lord Mortlake was never anything more to me than an amusement. One of those utterly tedious amusements one only finds at an English country house on an English country Sunday. I don’t think any one at all morally responsible for what he or she does at an English country house.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Yes. I know lots of people think that.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: I loved you, Arthur.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: My dear Mrs. Cheveley, you have always been far too clever to know anything about love.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: I did love you. And you loved me. You know you loved me; and love is a very wonderful thing. I suppose that when a man has once loved a woman, he will do anything for her, except continue to love her?
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Puts her hand on his .
Taking his hand away quietly .
Yes: except that.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: After a pause .

I am tired of living abroad. I want to come back to London. I want to have a charming house here. I want to have a salon. If one could only teach the English how to talk, and the Irish how to listen, society here would be quite civilised. Besides, I have arrived at the romantic stage. When I saw you last night at the Chilterns’, I knew you were the only person I had ever cared for, if I ever have cared for anybody, Arthur. And so, on the morning of the day you marry me, I will give you Robert Chiltern’s letter. That is my offer. I will give it to you now, if you promise to marry me.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Now?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Smiling .
To-morrow.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Are you really serious?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Yes, quite serious.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: I should make you a very bad husband.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: I don’t mind bad husbands. I have had two. They amused me immensely.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: You mean that you amused yourself immensely, don’t you?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: What do you know about my married life?
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Nothing: but I can read it like a book.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: What book?
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Rising .
The Book of Numbers.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Do you think it is quite charming of you to be so rude to a woman in your own house?
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: In the case of very fascinating women, sex is a challenge, not a defence.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: I suppose that is meant for a compliment. My dear Arthur, women are never disarmed by compliments. Men always are. That is the difference between the two sexes.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Women are never disarmed by anything, as far as I know them.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: After a pause .

Then you are going to allow your greatest friend, Robert Chiltern, to be ruined, rather than marry some one who really has considerable attractions left. I thought you would have risen to some great height of self-sacrifice, Arthur. I think you should. And the rest of your life you could spend in contemplating your own perfections.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY
